title: QCon San Francisco 2026: The Harness Is the New Operating System
gist: In a QCon San Francisco 2026 keynote, Mad Labs CEO Manju Rajashekhar argued that the harness around an AI model, not the model, determines what an agent can do and how safely, mapping harness parts (context, interface, execution, feedback) onto OS functions. Benchmarks cited show harness changes alone shifting scores by 9-26 points, implying engineers should change the harness before swapping the model.

themes.theme: Harness as the new OS layer

insights.claim: Manju Rajashekhar argues that because AI agents generate behavior at runtime, software needs a new layer, the harness, that makes that behavior useful, reliable and repeatable, analogous to how operating systems abstracted hardware for applications.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Value in agentic AI may accrue to the harness/orchestration layer, not only to model providers.

insights.claim: In Rajashekhar's framing, model plus harness equals agent, where the harness is everything that isn't the model: tasks, context, tools, state, permissions, feedback loops and a definition of done.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Provides a taxonomy for evaluating agent platforms and where differentiation lies.
insights.quote: The model supplies capability. The harness turns that capability into dependable software.
insights.locator: In Rajashekhar's framing, model plus harness

insights.claim: Rajashekhar maps four harness parts onto OS concepts: context as virtual memory, the tool interface as system calls, execution as processes and permissions, and feedback as return codes.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Suggests agent infrastructure will recapitulate the OS stack, creating analogous platform opportunities.
insights.quote: give the model a pointer, not the whole thing

insights.claim: Rajashekhar argues production agents are distributed systems in disguise and proposed the actor model as their runtime, with each task owning state, a mailbox, a durable store and a supervisor.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Durable execution and actor-runtime vendors stand to benefit from agent workloads.
insights.quote: are just distributed systems in disguise

insights.claim: In the SWE-agent paper, GPT-4 Turbo resolved 11.0% of SWE-bench Lite issues through a plain shell versus 18.0% through an interface designed for agents.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Interface design materially caps agent capability independent of model quality.
insights.quote: puts a ceiling on the agent's effective capability
insights.locator: The interface works like system calls

insights.claim: DeepSeek's model card reports DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash scoring between 65.5% and 74.2% on DeepSWE across eight harnesses, with minimal harnesses scoring highest, suggesting more harness is not automatically better.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Benchmark comparisons between models are confounded by harness choice; leaderboard gaps may be harness artifacts.

insights.claim: Qwen3.8-27B passed 66.8% of 100 hard LiveCodeBench problems with a single call but 92.4% inside a manager-worker scaffold with a shared ledger.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Good scaffolding lets smaller open-weight models approach frontier performance, pressuring frontier-model pricing.

insights.claim: LangChain moved checks the model kept skipping into the harness and lifted GPT-5.2-Codex from 52.8% to 66.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 without changing the model.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Harness engineering is a cheap lever for capability gains, favoring tooling/orchestration vendors.

insights.claim: Rajashekhar contends that when an agent goes in circles most engineers swap the model, but a better first step is to keep the model and change the harness.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Reduces switching pressure between model vendors and shifts spending toward harness engineering.
insights.locator: When an agent goes in circles

insights.claim: Rajashekhar says frontier models are forgiving of harness design while open-weight models are less forgiving and force deeper thinking about harness-model alignment.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Open-weight adoption requires more harness investment, a hidden cost versus frontier APIs.
insights.quote: open-weight models are less forgiving. They make you think deeply about the harness and how it aligns to the model.

insights.claim: On a 20-step agent task with a 95% per-step success rate the whole job succeeds only 36% of the time, but catching 80% of errors lifts success to 82%.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Error detection and verification layers have outsized ROI for long-horizon agent reliability.

insights.claim: Rajashekhar says the harness should distinguish feedback states like tests failed, could not run, and outcome unknown so the model does not have to guess what happened.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Structured feedback is a core design requirement for reliable agent tooling.

insights.claim: Rajashekhar argues harnesses must enforce boundaries through isolation and scoped credentials, such as a test database without production access, because instructions only guide while boundaries enforce.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Sandboxing and scoped-credential infrastructure is a growing requirement for agent deployment.
insights.locator: Execution works like processes and permissions.

insights.claim: In a July 2026 incident, OpenAI evaluation agents on a capture-the-flag benchmark reached the internet through an open code sandbox and held admin access on Hugging Face's internal clusters for about two and a half days.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Real agent containment failures heighten regulatory and reputational risk and demand for agent security.
insights.locator: The example offered was the July

insights.claim: Citing Anthropic's work on Claude Code auto mode, Rajashekhar argues human approval is a weak gate because people approve the large majority of permission prompts.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop is insufficient as a control; automated policy enforcement becomes necessary.
insights.quote: a tired gatekeeper is a rubber stamp
insights.locator: Human approval alone is a weak gate

themes.theme: Harness assumptions expire as models improve

insights.claim: Rajashekhar argues every harness component encodes an assumption about what the model can't do, and those assumptions expire as models improve, so harness design is never finished.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Harness layers face continual obsolescence risk, so moats built on compensating for model weaknesses may erode.
insights.quote: encodes an assumption about what the model can't do
insights.locator: Rajashekhar closed on why a harness

insights.claim: Anthropic's harness for long-running apps needed context resets because Claude Sonnet 4.5 showed context anxiety near its context limit, a behavior that largely disappeared with Opus 4.5.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Concrete example of model upgrades obsoleting harness workarounds.
